basic_information.short_title: General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, FY 2023
basic_information.official_title: AN ACT APPROPRIATING FUNDS FOR THE OPERATION OF THE BANGSAMORO GOVERNMENT FROM JANUARY ONE TO DECEMBER THIRTY-ONE, TWO THOUSAND AND TWENTY-THREE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: The region's ₱85.36 billion budget for 2023 — the first budget of the reconstituted Bangsamoro Transition Authority, published under the theme “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro”.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: The Bangsamoro Government requires an annual appropriations act to operate. This one covers 1 January to 31 December 2023 and was the first written by the Parliament reconstituted after the transition period was extended.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: ₱85,359,315,687.00 is appropriated from the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. The act funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 5 special purpose funds, and carries 73 sections of general provisions.
who_will_be_affected: Everyone in the region, through the ministries and services this funds
Constituent local government units, through a ₱2.30 billion support fund
All Bangsamoro Government personnel, whose allowances, honoraria and bonuses it sets
Contractors and suppliers, through procurement and disclosure rules
Teachers, resource persons and staff on special projects, through honoraria

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: This is a money law: it decides how much funding BARMM ministries and programs get - the schools, hospitals, roads, scholarships, and social services you use are all paid from it. No single citizen 'applies' for it, but nearly every public service you touch depends on it.
in_practice: Sets each ministry's budget ceiling for the year (or adds/extends funds mid-year for supplementals and extensions)
Slow disbursement is the recurring issue - several BAAs exist purely to extend the validity of unspent funds
Big-ticket items to watch: education (MBHTE), health (MOH), public works (MPW), and the Special Development Fund for conflict-affected communities

for_specific_groups.Parents & students: Classroom construction, teacher hiring, and scholarship slots are set here
for_specific_groups.Patients: Hospital operating budgets, medicines, and health worker salaries flow from this law
for_specific_groups.Workers & suppliers: Government projects and procurement opportunities follow the appropriations
for_specific_groups.Taxpayers: This is the accountability document - compare what was appropriated with what was actually delivered

watch_out_for: A law appropriating funds is a promise on paper: actual services depend on the budget being released and spent - ask the implementing ministry for the implementation timeline.
Follow-up reports: the Parliament itself has passed resolutions demanding ministries account for these funds
Already amended by BAA 52 - read the consolidated text
what_this_means_for_you.when_you_will_feel_it: Laws take effect shortly after publication, but felt impact follows budgets, IRRs, and agency rollout - typically months, not days
what_you_can_do: Ask your municipal/barangay office or the implementing ministry how and when it will roll out where you live
Read the full text (PDF) on the Parliament's website or the Official Gazette of the Bangsamoro - the final sections say when it takes effect and who must act
If it isn't being implemented, raise it with your Member of Parliament or through the ministry's public assistance desk

key_terms_explained.BAA: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act - a regional law passed by the Bangsamoro Parliament, applying inside BARMM alongside national laws.
key_terms_explained.IRR: Implementing Rules and Regulations - the ministry-issued 'how-to' that turns a law's text into procedures; many laws only bite once the IRR is out.
key_terms_explained.GAA: General Appropriations Act - the annual budget law deciding how much each ministry and program gets.

benefits.headline: Funds every public service you use - the enabler of all other benefits.

direct_benefits.benefit: Operating budgets for schools, hospitals, roads, scholarships, social programs
Salaries of teachers, health workers, and government personnel
Special Development Fund projects in conflict-affected communities

indirect_benefits: Procurement and job opportunities from funded projects
Predictability: agencies can plan the year
limitations: Benefits arrive only as fast as funds are released and the implementing office organizes - expect a lag between enactment and service.
Compare appropriations vs. actual delivery - Parliament's own resolutions demand these reports; you can too

key_provisions: Section 1 — Appropriation of Funds. ₱85,359,315,687.00 is appropriated “out of the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, share in the National Government taxes, fees and charges collected in the Bangsamoro territorial jurisdiction, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges” for the operation of the Bangsamoro Government from 1 January to 31 December 2023. The published volume carries the theme “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro”.

Bangsamoro Government Budget — The act funds 17 ministries and 11 other executive offices: the Office of the Wali, the Youth, Women and Sports Commissions, the Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, the Planning and Development Authority, the Attorney-General's Office, the Pilgrimage Authority, the Cooperatives and Social Enterprise Authority, the Development Academy of the Bangsamoro and the Human Rights Commission. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱3,939,145,853.00, or 4.6% of the total: General Administration and Support ₱468,607,610, Support to Operations ₱377,132,711 and Operations ₱3,093,405,532. Within Operations the act itemises a Legislation line of ₱364,640,000, Representations/Constituency Building ₱1,026,816,000, Special Legislature Activities ₱267,840,000, Community Upliftment ₱120,000,000, Oversight ₱104,544,000, a Parliamentary Learning Program ₱40,000,000 and a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum ₱10,000,000; Personnel Services of ₱1,159,565,532 sits in the Operations total without being distributed across those sub-programmes.

Special purpose funds — The Pension and Gratuity Fund is ₱300,627,840.00 and the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund ₱2,615,269,253.00, nearly 4 times its FY 2022 level. The Contingent Fund is ₱5,029,839,521.00, earmarking ₱2,800,000,000 for a Transitional Development Impact Fund and again allowing use for the “cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs”. The Special Development Fund holds at ₱5,000,000,000.00 and the Local Government Support Fund rises to ₱2,297,491,000.00.

Sections 2–14 (Receipts and Income) — The act itself serves as the allotment order except for appropriations with pre-release conditions, lump sums without release details, and items requiring a Special Budget. Fees, charges and revenues are remitted to the Bangsamoro Treasury under Section 3, Chapter I, Book VII of BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, and form part of the general fund, with the schedule of fees posted on ministry websites and displayed in big bold characters in every provincial, municipal and field office. Foreign grants require prior clearance from the President. Trust receipts, performance bonds, public-private partnership receipts and revolving funds are separately regulated, with revolving funds barred from paying discretionary and representation expenses. Section 10 requires the Treasury to publish information on all Special Accounts and Funds. National internal revenue taxes and import duties on foreign donations, grants and loans are deemed automatically appropriated.

Sections 15–24 (Expenditure) — Procurement follows existing government procurement law, with early procurement activities authorised. Section 18, new this year, requires all ministries and offices to buy their common-use supplies from the Procurement Service under L.O.I. No. 755, E.O. No. 359 s. 1989 and A.O. No. 17 s. 2011. Amounts for information and communications technology equipment must be used to provide officials and employees with personal computers, operating systems, basic software and other essential electronic devices. Supply inventories are capped at a 3-month requirement. Infrastructure projects may not be sited in critical geohazard areas or no-build zones, must meet the structural strength and climate resilience standards set by the Ministry of Public Works, and must minimise biodiversity loss within the National Integrated Protected Area System; Section 21 also introduces a cap, allowing ministries to deduct engineering and administrative overhead of no more than 1% of project funds for infrastructure projects costing more than ₱1,000,000. Rainwater collection systems are required in public markets, school sites and government buildings. A Certification of Availability of Funds is required before any obligation, and a Multi-Year Contractual Authority before any multi-year contract.

Sections 25–33 (Cross-cutting programmes) — Every ministry and office must formulate a Gender and Development Plan integrated into its regular activities amounting to at least 5% of its budget, following RA 9710, the Magna Carta of Women. Ministries must address senior citizens and persons with disability, and all government infrastructure must include accessibility features. Section 28 continues the direction to mainstream Islamic or Shari'ah-compliant finance, with the Chief Minister to promulgate guidelines on the recommendation of the Technical Working Group on Islamic Finance. Built heritage and cultural landscapes may be altered only with the Chief Minister's prior approval. Disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation must be built into projects, energy efficiency measures adopted, biodiversity protected, and structures in seismically vulnerable areas repaired and retrofitted.

Sections 34–49 (Personnel benefits) — Section 34 caps Personnel Services for one fiscal year at 45% of the Bangsamoro Government's total revenue sources, under Section 6, Article XII of RA 11054. Section 36 sets annual extraordinary expenses at ₱264,000 for the Chief Minister, ₱108,000 for each Deputy Chief Minister, the Speaker and each Member of the Parliament, ₱45,600 for each Minister, ₱26,400 for each Deputy Minister or Bangsamoro Director-General and ₱19,200 for each Director II or Director III, with miscellaneous expenses of up to ₱90,000 for each of their offices. Section 40 provides that deductions may never reduce an employee's monthly net take-home pay below ₱5,000. Section 41 grants PERA of ₱2,000 a month; Section 42 a uniform or clothing allowance of up to ₱6,000 a year. Section 44 grants hazard duty pay only to personnel assigned to “strife-torn or embattled areas as may be determined and certified by the Secretary of National Defense”. Section 45, new this year, sets out who may receive honoraria — teachers working outside regular hours, lecturers and resource persons, members of boards and councils not paid salaries or per diems, science and technology personnel working beyond their load, and officials on reform-oriented special projects, whose total honoraria may not exceed 25% of their annual basic salaries. Section 46 sets monthly representation and transportation allowances at ₱14,000 for the Chief Minister, ₱11,000 for Deputy Chief Ministers, the Speaker and Members of the Parliament, ₱9,000 for Ministers, ₱8,500 for Deputy Ministers, ₱7,500 for Director II and Director III and ₱5,000 for Chiefs of Division and Director I. Sections 47 and 48 grant a mid-year bonus of 1 month's basic salary and a year-end bonus of 1 month plus a ₱5,000 cash gift.

Sections 50–63 (Release and use of funds) — Section 50 makes appropriations available for release and disbursement until 31 December 2023, while the local government support fund released and obligated during the fiscal year may be disbursed until 31 December 2024. Infrastructure capital outlays must be completed, inspected and paid by 30 June 2024, and MOOE and other capital outlays delivered, inspected and paid by 31 March 2024. New this year: funds transferred between organisational units, between ministries, or to local government units “shall not be considered disbursed under this Section until the transferred amounts have been actually utilized to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered, inspected and accepted within the validity period” — closing the practice of counting a transfer as spending. Unreleased appropriations lapse and unexpended funds revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation under Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054. Only the Chief Minister and the Speaker may declare and use savings, and only to augment actual deficiencies in existing items of their own appropriations. Cash advances may not be granted until earlier ones are liquidated, and an Annual Report on Cash Advances naming the recipients must go to the Committee on Finance, and Budget and Management.

Sections 64–74 (Administrative procedures and final provisions) — Foreign travel of Ministers, Heads of Offices and officials at salary grade 25 and above requires clearance from the Office of the Chief Minister. Section 67 requires a status report to the Commission on Audit within 60 days of receiving its Annual Audit Report, published on the ministry's website. Section 69 requires quarterly financial and physical reports, with failure resulting in “the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until they have complied”. Section 70 requires publication of each infrastructure project's title, location, description, estimates, winning contractor and bid within 30 calendar days of contract, and of its detailed actual cost and any variation orders within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion. Section 71 cautions any court, ministry or office against garnishing or subjecting public funds to levy and execution. Section 72 makes payment for the Personnel Services of employees absorbed under Section 10, Article XVI of RA 11054 without prejudice to a funding request to the National Government. Section 74 sets effectivity at 1 January 2023.

impact.figures_note: Grand total quoted from Section 1. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority's ₱3,939,145,853 is 4.6% of that total. The Contingent Fund is ₱5,029,839,521.00, the Special Development Fund ₱5,000,000,000.00, the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund ₱2,615,269,253.00, the Local Government Support Fund ₱2,297,491,000.00 and the Pension and Gratuity Fund ₱300,627,840.00. Personnel Services across government are capped at 45% of total revenue sources, at least 5% of every ministry and office budget must go to gender-responsive programmes, and engineering and administrative overhead on infrastructure projects over ₱1,000,000 is capped at 1%.

amended_by: BAA 52 (2023) — extending the validity of the FY 2023 appropriations to 31 December 2024, amending Section 50
related_legislation.related_note: Funding sources and the 45% Personnel Services ceiling derive from Sections 6 and 19 of Article XII of RA 11054, the Organic Law; the ₱5 billion annual Special Development Fund comes from Article XIV of the same law. Remittance of agency income follows Section 3, Chapter I, Book VII of BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code. Section 72 gives effect to Section 10, Article XVI of RA 11054 on absorbed employees. Gender and development follows RA 9710 and reports flow to the Bangsamoro Women Commission created by BAA 8. Common-use supplies procurement follows L.O.I. No. 755, E.O. No. 359 s. 1989 and A.O. No. 17 s. 2011. BAA 84, the Bangsamoro Budget System Act of 2025, later codified as permanent law many of the rules this act carried annually.

citizen_questions.q: How big was the 2023 regional budget?
citizen_questions.a: ₱85,359,315,687.00, covering 1 January to 31 December 2023 — 6.9% more than the year before. The published volume carries the theme “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro”.

citizen_questions.q: Where did the money come from?
citizen_questions.a: The annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges.

₱3,939,145,853 through the Bangsamoro Transition Authority — 4.6% of the whole budget. Within its ₱3.09 billion Operations line the act itemises Representations/Constituency Building at ₱1,026,816,000, Special Legislature Activities at ₱267,840,000, Community Upliftment at ₱120,000,000, Oversight at ₱104,544,000, a Parliamentary Learning Program at ₱40,000,000 and a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum at ₱10,000,000, against a Legislation line of ₱364,640,000. Personnel Services of ₱1,159,565,532 is not distributed across those sub-programmes.

A Local Government Support Fund of ₱2,297,491,000, up from ₱1,394,016,000 the year before. Money from that fund released and obligated during 2023 could be disbursed until 31 December 2024, a year longer than the rest of the budget.

citizen_questions.q: Was there a limit on salaries?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Section 34 caps Personnel Services for one fiscal year at 45% of the Bangsamoro Government's total revenue sources, following Section 6, Article XII of RA 11054.

Section 45, new this year, limits honoraria to teaching personnel working outside regular hours, lecturers and resource persons, members of boards and councils who receive no salary or per diem, science and technology personnel working beyond their load, and officials assigned to reform-oriented special projects — whose total honoraria from all such projects may not exceed 25% of their annual basic salaries.

citizen_questions.q: Is there a cap on project overheads?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Section 21 allows ministries to deduct engineering and administrative overhead of no more than 1% of project funds, and only for infrastructure projects costing more than ₱1,000,000. The cap appears for the first time in this act and has been carried in every budget since.

citizen_questions.q: Does transferring money to a local government count as spending it?
citizen_questions.a: No — not from this budget onward. Section 50 provides that funds transferred between organisational units, between ministries or to local government units are not considered disbursed “until the transferred amounts have been actually utilized to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered, inspected and accepted within the validity period”.

citizen_questions.q: What allowances did government employees get?
citizen_questions.a: PERA of ₱2,000 a month, a uniform or clothing allowance of up to ₱6,000 a year, a mid-year bonus of 1 month's salary and a year-end bonus of 1 month plus a ₱5,000 cash gift. Deductions could never reduce monthly net take-home pay below ₱5,000.

citizen_questions.q: How long was the money available?
citizen_questions.a: Until 31 December 2023, with construction completed and paid by 30 June 2024 and other deliveries paid by 31 March 2024. Parliament then extended it by BAA 52 to 31 December 2024.

views.simple: The region's ₱85.36 billion budget for 2023, themed “Optimizing the budget towards a transformative Bangsamoro” — the first written by the reconstituted Bangsamoro Transition Authority. It funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 5 special purpose funds, and carries 73 sections of operating rules: Personnel Services capped at 45% of revenue, at least 5% of every budget for gender programmes, a new 1% ceiling on engineering and administrative overhead for projects over ₱1,000,000, a new rule that money transferred to another agency or a local government does not count as disbursed until it is actually spent, common-use supplies bought through the Procurement Service, honoraria limited to a defined list of recipients, a ₱5,000 net take-home pay floor, hazard duty pay certified by the Secretary of National Defense, published contracts and actual costs for every infrastructure project, and automatic salary suspension for officials who fail to report.
